match.reason: The closest bank point, ecb-rights-responsibilities, teaches rights and responsibilities for both consumers and businesses and only touches on one consumer responsibility, so it is broader than the new point, which covers only consumer responsibilities: reading terms, keeping receipts, using products as intended and complaining through the right channels.

draft.title: Consumer responsibilities
card: Consumers have rights, and they also have responsibilities. Meeting them helps buyers protect themselves and makes it easier to sort out a problem.
Read the terms
Before agreeing to buy or sign up, read the terms and conditions. They set out the price, the length of the deal and any rules or extra charges.
Keep receipts
A receipt is proof of purchase. It shows what you bought, when and how much you paid, so keep it in case something goes wrong.
Use and complain properly
Use a product the way it is meant to be used. If there is a problem, take it first to the seller, then to a consumer agency if it is not fixed.
draft.remember: Read the terms, keep receipts, use products as intended, and complain through the right channels.

a.q: Why should a consumer keep the receipt after buying a pair of headphones?
opts: It is proof of purchase if the headphones are faulty
It lets the shop change the price of the headphones later
It stops the headphones from developing any faults
It is needed before the headphones can be used
a.why: A receipt shows what was bought, when and for how much, so the buyer can prove the purchase if there is a problem. It does not prevent faults or affect how the product works.
a.clue: Think about what you must show the seller if something goes wrong.

b.q: Zara's new blender stops working. She used it to crush large blocks of ice, but the instructions say it is for soft foods only. Which responsibility did Zara not meet?
opts: Using the product as it is meant to be used
Reading the terms before agreeing to buy
Keeping the receipt as proof of purchase
Complaining through the right channels
b.why: The instructions say the blender is for soft foods, and Zara used it on large ice blocks. That means she did not use it as intended. The other options are not mentioned in the case, so we cannot say she missed them.
b.clue: Compare what the instructions say with what Zara did.

a.best: It is proof of purchase if the headphones are faulty

b.best: Using the product as it is meant to be used

problems.detail: The clue says 'what you must show the seller', which implies a receipt is required. Under the Australian Consumer Law any proof of purchase (such as a bank statement) can do, and the card only says to keep it 'in case something goes wrong'.

The three wrong options are plainly absurd (a receipt is needed to use headphones, stops faults, lets the shop change the price). The right option is also the only one using the card's phrase 'proof of purchase', so students can pick it without understanding the idea.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. Question a's distractors are too obviously wrong, and its clue's 'must show' overstates that a receipt is required.

proposal.title: Consumer responsibilities
card: Consumers have rights under the law, and they also have responsibilities. Meeting them helps buyers protect themselves and makes it easier to sort out a problem.
Read the terms
Before agreeing to buy or sign up, read the terms and conditions. They set out the price, the length of the deal and any rules or extra charges.
Keep receipts
A receipt shows what you bought, where, when and for how much. Keep it, or other proof such as a bank statement, so you can show a seller you bought the item.
Use and complain properly
Use a product the way it is meant to be used. If there is a problem, take it first to the seller, then to a consumer agency if it is not fixed.
proposal.remember: Read the terms, keep proof of purchase, use products as intended, and complain through the right channels.

a.q: Ben buys headphones, and a week later one side stops working. How does keeping his receipt help him?
opts: It helps him show he bought them from that shop
It proves the fault was not caused by him
It is the only proof the shop has to accept
It is what gives him the right to have them fixed
a.why: A receipt records what was bought, where, when and for how much, so it helps Ben show the shop sold him the headphones. It says nothing about how he used them, so it cannot prove the fault was not his doing. His rights come from the law, and other proof such as a bank statement can also show the purchase.
a.clue: Think about the details a receipt records.
